name: Ricky McCormick's encrypted notes
date: found 30 June 1999 (McCormick's body found near St. Louis, Missouri; notes found in his pocket, allegedly written 'no more than three days before his death')

note_1: WLD RCCBRNSE NT SSNENTXSE-CRSLE-CLTRSE WLD NCBE

ciphertext_source: Cipherbrain post 10 (Schmeh 2018, sources/schmeh/posts/10-mccormick.txt), 'Transcriptions' section: Schmeh's own re-transcription of the two notes from the FBI's photographs (FBI published the two encrypted messages on its website 30 March 2011, twelve years after the notes were found). Kept as two separate note_1/note_2 arrays (13 and 17 lines) since they are physically separate notes, not one continuous text.
alphabet: mixed uppercase Latin letters, digits, hyphens, slashes, periods, parentheses, a question mark and an apostrophe; the recurring token 'NCBE' appears roughly 20 times across both notes and is the most distinctive repeated element

constraints.history: FBI's own codebreaking unit (CRRU, which has 'a success rate of about 99 percent' per Schmeh) and the American Cryptogram Association (ACA) both failed to solve it; the FBI ran a public online forum after the 2011 release specifically to manage the volume of amateur submissions
constraints.author_background: McCormick had no formal cryptology education and no known interest in computers or mathematics, but family members told police he had 'occupied himself with encryption since his childhood' and never explained his methods to them
constraints.hypothesis_note: the heavy use of repeated multi-letter tokens (NCBE, and endings like -RSE/-MRSE/-NSE) is consistent with either a personal phonetic/shorthand system (not a classical substitution cipher) or a nomenclator-style code; this is an open hypothesis in the source, not established

cheap_tests_in_order: 1. Catalogue every repeated 2+ character token across both notes (NCBE, -RSE family, WLD, etc.) with position and frequency, and compare the resulting token-frequency profile against known personal-shorthand and phonetic-spelling systems (e.g. Gregg shorthand transliterated to Latin letters, or simple vowel-dropping schemes) rather than assuming a classical letter substitution. Cost $1, Sonnet.

2. (Restated 25 Sept 2026 by LANE B2 for NEAR.md row mccormick-1999.) Simple substitution of a vowel-dropped English: tools/family_run.py specs/mccormick-1999.json --family masc, run twice -- once with the default English corpus and once with --corpus pointing at a vowel-dropped English corpus built from tools/data (vowels removed word-internally, word-initial vowels kept); each run's control is built by the tool at N=746 and the spec's K, 3 seeds, gate 0.6; report control recovery and target judge line side by side for both corpora, plus the test-1 controls' numbers for reference. Cost $5, Sonnet. (Earlier wording, kept: 2. Index-of-coincidence and letter-frequency test on the folded (letters-only) text against English, with a matched control: synthetic English plaintext passed through the same 'strip non-letters, keep the token structure' folding at the same N (367 and 379 letters), same solver. Given the heavy rep...)

3. Treat NCBE (and other frequent tokens) as candidate code-words in a small personal nomenclator and attempt a constrained substitution search using only the token vocabulary actually present (not a full 26-letter MASC), scored by word-cover against English after the substitution -- this is the FBI/ACA's own presumed approach and failed publicly, so expect a negative; report it as such rather than re-running it uncritically. Cost $2-3.
matched_control: not yet run; test 2 above proposes the design (synthetic English plaintext, same folding, same N, same solver)

1.method: specs/cheap-tests/mccormick-1999/run_test1.py (LANE B2 worker bMCC): catalogued every repeated token (2+ letters, split on any non-letter char) across both notes with position/count, plus a substring-occurrence count for the top 20 (specs/cheap-tests/mccormick-1999/top20_tokens.tsv); computed vowel share, share of letters covered by a repeated n-gram (n=3..6), and IC on the letters-only fold, combined N=746 (note1=367, note2=379), against 3-seed matched controls at the same N cut from tools/data/pg1661_holmes.txt (no network fetch): (A) real English prose, (B) the same English with vowels dropped, (C) the same English letters shuffled. No decipherment attempted.
1.reading: the notes' repeated-n-gram coverage and IC sit above all three controls at every n (3..6), including above the vowel-dropped shorthand control; vowel share sits below real English prose, closer to (but distinctly above) the vowel-dropped control's zero. This is consistent with the source's own stated hypothesis (heavy reuse of a small token vocabulary -- NCBE, the -RSE family, WLD -- more like a personal shorthand or nomenclator than a 1:1 substitution of ordinary English letter frequencies), not a decipherment or a claim about what the tokens mean (rule 10). Substring occurrences of NCBE (18, vs 11 as a delimiter-isolated token) confirm it also appears embedded inside longer undelimited runs, close to the source's 'roughly 20 times' note.

2.method: LANE B2 worker bMCC2: tools/family_run.py specs/mccormick-1999.json --family masc --cipher specs/cheap-tests/mccormick-1999/cipher_both_notes.txt --tokens letters --seeds 3 --gate 0.6, run twice -- once with the default English corpus (--corpus tools/data/pg1661_holmes.txt --corpus tools/data/pg2701_mobydick.txt) and once with the vowel-dropped English corpus built for this test (--corpus tools/data/en_vdrop, built by tools/data/en_vdrop/build_en_vdrop.py: word-initial vowels kept, word-internal a/e/i/o/u dropped, from the same two source texts, no network fetch). Both runs use --tokens letters (auto mode would pick 'space' here because the spec's ciphertext mixes letters with digits/punctuation/hyphens; --tokens letters reproduces test 1's letters-only fold, N=746, K=24 distinct). Rows in ciphers/mccormick-1999/HYPOTHESES.md.

control_recovery.test1_reference_ic_only: test 1's own controls were a different design (IC/n-gram-coverage/vowel-share statistics, not a solved-recovery fraction): IC 0.0674 (prose), 0.0823 (no-vowel), 0.0674 (shuffled) vs notes 0.08927; not directly comparable to this test's recovery fractions, kept here only because the brief asked for the test-1 numbers alongside test 2's for reference.

target_judge.default_english: judge PASS (tools/judge_plaintext.py specs/mccormick-1999.json --file ciphers/mccormick-1999/families/masc-1.txt, run via family_run.py; a PASS is a gate for a verifier, not a reading, rule 10)
target_judge.vowel_dropped_english: judge PASS (same command against the vowel-dropped-corpus run's decode)

2.caveat: Both controls sit at or above the ~0.95 near-ceiling line CLAUDE.md rule 3 warns has 'no headroom to show a gain regardless of the technique' -- a masc anneal at N=746, K=24 (restarts=8) essentially always recovers a random simple-substitution key at this length, for both the plain and vowel-dropped English designs. Both target decodes (ciphers/mccormick-1999/families/masc-1.txt, overwritten by each run in turn -- see the run's own date/corpus header line inside the file) read as letter salad with no recognisable English words, despite the judge PASS: e.g. run 1 opens 'hanheathestasiheahethtsh / deatalastalestereeastalestoar'; run 2 opens 'htdhmtthrsttsnhmthrthtsh / grtttltsttlsstrhsststtlrstwth'. This is consistent with the judge's own documented limitation for this target (schema_note above: 'no language check is meaningful yet given the token structure'): the heavy repeated-token structure the notes already carry (NCBE, -RSE family, test 1) drives n-gram likelihood up under any consistent key, independent of whether the key is right, so a PASS here is not evidence of a real simple-substitution decipherment under either English design. Neither run supports the source's competing hypothesis (personal shorthand/nomenclator, not 1:1 letter substitution) over the null; a bespoke tokenizer-aware judge (test 1's schema_note) remains the more promising next step, not a straight masc anneal at this N.

value: medium: a famous, extensively studied FBI-failed target (CRRU's ~99% success rate makes this a genuine outlier), but the mixed alphanumeric/punctuation structure means a standard classical-cipher judge is only weakly applicable; any reading here needs a bespoke tokenizer, not a straight letters-only fold
status_25_Sept_2026: open (FBI released the notes 30 March 2011, most recent FBI statement referenced by the survey is Nov 2025); FBI CRRU and ACA both failed
schema_note: cheap_tests_in_order are proposals (rule 10: an approach is not a claim); a test actually run goes under cheap_test_done with its control. judge block uses only letters_min/max on the folded (letters-only, punctuation/digits stripped) text as a placeholder; no 'language' check is meaningful yet given the token structure (NCBE etc.) -- a bespoke tokenizer-aware judge would be a better long-term fit than tools/judge_plaintext.py's plain letter n-gram model, and is left as a follow-up, not built here (scope of this brief).
